source.title: Understanding deep learning (still) requires rethinking generalization
source.authors: Chiyuan Zhang; Samy Bengio; Moritz Hardt; B. Recht; O. Vinyals

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the complete paper text, including appendices; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: It directly trains image classifiers on natural and randomized labels, compares their train and test performance, and varies explicit regularization.
record.gate_note: Results cited from other work are not rows. The finite-sample expressivity theorem is theoretical and not an experimental result row. The kernel experiments are recorded because the paper reports their test errors, but they do not test a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The supplied text is Zhang et al.'s original V1 study, despite the different record DOI. It directly compares natural-label generalization with fixed-random-label fitting. Its CIFAR-10 results also compare convolutional and fully connected networks, bearing on V3. The bundled ImageNet regularizer changes do not identify dropout's effect for V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the tested networks can memorize randomized labels while generalizing on natural labels, and architecture-level complexity measures and explicit regularization alone do not explain this coexistence. The authors also emphasize that easy optimization and successful generalization require different explanations.
record.recipe_differences: The study is the Zhang et al. random-label memorization and natural-label generalization study named in V1; it reports experiments on CIFAR10 and ImageNet and additionally varies explicit regularizers.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, architecture, label corruption, data augmentation, weight decay, dropout, and batch normalization are varied or compared. Batch normalization is associated with a reported 3–4% generalization impact in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Unregularized kernel interpolation achieves test errors of 1.2% and 0.6% on MNIST, and 46% and 17% on CIFAR-10, depending on preprocessing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel interpolators can generalize on image benchmarks without explicit regularization, with substantial sensitivity to their representation.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing dropout and weight decay together with augmentation retained lowers ImageNet top-1 test accuracy from 77.84% to 72.95%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bundled dropout and weight decay improve Inception V3 accuracy in this augmented ImageNet recipe; their individual contributions are unidentified.

record.problems: The ImageNet random-label experiment does not reach perfect training accuracy. CIFAR10 results give no uncertainty estimates. Some ImageNet table entries are flattened and top-1 training values are not recoverable for two configurations. Early-stopping performance is described by the authors as potential because a separate validation procedure is needed.
record.rows_left_out: No reported qualifying result rows were omitted. The text also reports label-corruption curves and random-pixel fitting in figures, but exact condition-specific values are figure-only; their broader descriptions are captured in page excerpts and the reported table rows cover the direct natural-versus-random label results.

untested.parts: No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No isolation of local connectivity, learned sparse connections, convolutional initialization transfer, or datasets beyond CIFAR-10.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No isolated dropout effect, very small training-set comparison, excessive-dropout sweep, or augmentation setting where removing dropout and weight decay together preserves or improves accuracy.
No magnitude-aware perturbation measure or ranking of generalization gaps within a convolutional family.
No removal and retraining experiment based on example memorization.

missing.what: Random-label fitting with explicit regularization: weight decay gives 100% training accuracy for Inception and MLP 3x512, 99.21% for MLP 1x512, while AlexNet fails to converge. Inception reaches 99.93% with random cropping and 99.28% with augmentation after a changed schedule and longer training. These are additional conditions, not replacements for the unregularized rows; augmented training accuracy is an online average over changing inputs.
missing.locator: Section 3; Appendix E, Table 4 and accompanying text

record.verdict_notes: No V1 verdict is issued because the supplied text is the original arXiv:1611.03530 study named in V1. The record's V6 limits_scope verdict mistakes an unidentified dropout contribution for an observed limitation. Figure-only corruption and random-pixel results were already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests CIFAR-10 models and Inception V3 on ImageNet, but not every architecture and setting named in the version.
The ImageNet table reports bundled regularizer settings; it does not isolate dropout’s effect while holding other conditions fixed, nor test very small training sets or excessive dropout.

tranche.reason: The CACM article republishes the original experiment and reports the same randomization method and accuracy measures. It is overlapping evidence, not an independent replication.

source_check.notes: The DOI 10.1145/3446776 article is the 2021 CACM republication by Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht, and Vinyals. The named pdfs/text file instead contains the 2017 original version, with a different author order and publication identity. Use the CACM article for this DOI; do not import its referenced 2017 appendix values as if printed in the 2021 article.

statements.correction: CACM Table 1 reports natural-label Inception train/test accuracy of 100.0%/85.75% and random-label accuracy of 100.0%/9.78%; random-label training accuracy is 99.82% for Alexnet, 100.0% for MLP 3 × 512, and 99.34% for MLP 1 × 512. Section 2.1 reports 95.20% top-1 accuracy for random-label ImageNet Inception V3 and says it is below 100%. The 0.11% test value and detailed protocol are in the referenced 2017 Appendix Table 2, not reported directly in CACM.
statements.problem: The CACM article reports the CIFAR-10 Table 1 values and the 95.20% ImageNet random-label accuracy. It does not report the 0.11% ImageNet test value or explicitly give its full cell-specific condition; it points to Zhang et al. 2017 Appendix Table 2. The CACM article identifies itself as a republication, not an independent replication.
